desc:
You stand on index 0 of nums and want to reach index nums.length - 1. From index i you may leap to any index j with i < j ≤ i + k (and j inside the array). Your score is the sum of nums[i] over every index you stand on, including the first and the last one.

Return the maximum score over all possible routes.

nums = [3, -5, -2, 6, -9, 4], k = 2
route 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 5: 3 + (-5) + 6 + 4 = 8
route 0 -> 2 -> 3 -> 5: 3 + (-2) + 6 + 4 = 11
result = 11
hints: Let best[i] be the highest score of a route that ends on index i. What does best[i] depend on?
best[i] = nums[i] + max(best[j]) over the previous indices j with i - k ≤ j < i. Evaluating this maximum by scanning gives O(n * k).
The maximum of best over the last k indices is a sliding window maximum. Keep a deque of indices whose best values are decreasing, and pop the front when it is more than k behind.
editorial: Define best[0] = nums[0] and best[i] = nums[i] + max(best[j] for j in [i-k, i-1]). The answer is best[n-1]. The recurrence is a plain O(n * k) dynamic program, and the only slow part is the window maximum over the previous k states.

That window moves one step right per index, so a monotonic deque of indices (with decreasing best values) gives the maximum at its front in amortized O(1). Remove the front when its index is less than i - k, compute best[i], then pop smaller values from the back and push i. Total O(n) time and O(n) space (O(k) if only the deque is kept). Negative values are fine, since you must take the best predecessor even when it is negative.
solution:
def maxLeapScore(nums, k):
    from collections import deque
    n = len(nums)
    best = [0] * n
    best[0] = nums[0]
    dq = deque([0])
    for i in range(1, n):
        while dq[0] < i - k:
            dq.popleft()
        best[i] = nums[i] + best[dq[0]]
        while dq and best[dq[-1]] <= best[i]:
            dq.pop()
        dq.append(i)
    return best[-1]
